fields.title: What Requirements Mean Technically
fields.keyTakeaway: Regulatory requirements translate into architectural ones, and with proper design, compliance emerges naturally from product-driven decisions.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: A lawyer says "we need to comply with GDPR." What does that change in the product?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Regulatory requirements viewed as legal work result in a privacy policy on the website and nothing more. Real requirements are architectural, and retrofitting them post-facto takes quarters.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Main requirements and their technical meaning:
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Processing grounds.** Every type of processing has a legal basis. Technically—[[records-of-processing|records of processing activities]]: what, why, on what grounds, and how long it is stored.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Data subject rights.** Access, correction, deletion, portability. Technically—export, deletion across all systems, and data mapping from `SE2-N4-L2`.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **[[data-minimisation|Data minimization]].** Technically—field audits and retention periods.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **[[privacy-by-default|Privacy by default]].** Most secure settings without user action. Technically—consents are not pre-selected, visibility is minimal by default, and optional collection is turned off.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: **[[privacy-by-design|Privacy by design]].** Privacy is factored into design. Technically—a dedicated section in the spec and review prior to implementation.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: **[[breach-notification|Breach notification]].** The deadline is usually 72 hours. Technically—detection, impact assessment, procedure.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: **[[cross-border-transfer|Cross-border transfer]].** Restrictions on transferring data outside the jurisdiction. Technically—knowing the geography of all subprocessors, including the AI provider.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: **[[dpia|DPIA]]**—for high-risk processing: large-scale processing of sensitive data, systematic monitoring, and automated decisions about people.
fields.sections/2/blocks/9/text: Practical translation: **most requirements are what was described in the previous blocks.** Records, minimization, deletion, logs, subprocessor list. Compliance happens as a consequence of proper design, not as a separate project.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/3/1: Consents not pre-selected, three separate ones
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Almost no separate compliance work was required—it emerged from decisions made for product reasons.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: What was done specifically: processing registry as a document, DPIA for the personal recommendations feature, formalization of the notification procedure.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: The DPIA yielded an unexpected result: during the review, it turned out that recommendations used sensitive purchase categories as attributes. This led to the rule from `SE1-N3-L1`. The impact assessment worked as a design check rather than paperwork.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Requirements vary significantly across jurisdictions, and a product operating in multiple markets may not have a single configuration. This is an architectural constraint, not a legal detail.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Regulatory requirements translate into architectural ones, and with proper design, compliance emerges naturally from product-driven decisions.
